title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk
web_title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk
book_title: Chapter 5: Management on Trial — Leading KPIs & Walking the Talk
question: Which operating numbers tell you where Creative Newtech's profits and cash are heading before the income statement does, how much of the ₹6,000 Cr FY29 ambition is credible, and how often has management delivered what it said it would?

epigraph.quote: Creative’s business model is primarily of optimizing working capital. Success of our business depends on achieving higher growth through higher margin products and quick working capital cycle.
epigraph.author: Creative Newtech Limited, Q4 FY24 investor presentation, May 2024

web_blocks.text: Four operating numbers lead this company's financials by two to four quarters. They are gross margin, the share of revenue that comes from owned and licensed brands, net working capital days, and the ratio of operating cash flow to operating profit. Interest cost and returns on capital follow them. In H1 FY27 the first two moved the right way, and the last two swung hard enough to need a chapter of their own (Chapter 6). This chapter scores the leading indicators and tests the market-size claims that sit behind the ₹6,000 Cr FY29 target. It then audits what the CEO and CFO promised between 2022 and 2026 against what the filings later showed. The short answer is that management has delivered the numbers its profit and loss account controls and has repeatedly missed the numbers its balance sheet controls. [33][34]

Cover below 3x, which is Crisil's stated downgrade trigger [39]

web_blocks.takeaway: Gross margin, brand share and reported ROCE sit at or near multi-year highs in H1 FY27. The two indicators that measure funding stress moved in opposite directions: cash surged and interest cover fell to 3.8x. [29][33][31]

web_blocks.text: The margin gain is real, but read where it came from. In H1 FY27 the brand segment earned ₹72.90 Cr of contribution on ₹213.39 Cr of revenue. That is a 34% margin against 35.5% a year earlier, so brand margins were flat. The market-entry segment earned ₹67.59 Cr on ₹1,014.81 Cr, a 6.7% margin against 3.4%. That segment supplied about 65% of the ₹57.5 Cr increase in total segment contribution. [31] The CMD's explanation is that Make-in-India suppliers are smaller, so the margin is higher. He adds that ‘these are smaller customers, so they can't really have a lot of money for larger orders cash flow’. [34] We read that as a risk premium. Part of the margin gain is the price of lending to small principals and customers, and it should be read together with working capital rather than instead of it.

The brand KPI is narrower than it looks. Honeywell contributed ₹369.61 Cr of the ₹380.86 Cr brand segment in FY26 on the CFO's figure, about 97%. That runs under a licence that the CMD said in May 2025 would renew in December 2025. In May 2026 he said it would renew in March 2027. [34][36][30] He also said Honeywell is splitting into five companies, so the licensor's own structure is moving. [34] The diversifiers are early. WOZOYO sold about $2.2 million, roughly ₹20 Cr, in its first months in the US, with Amazon advertising running near 50% of sales. The chairman says three months; the sales window is about two. The AT&T licence signed on 12 November 2026 has no disclosed revenue yet. [32][42] Until those two carry revenue, ‘brand share’ is largely a measure of one licence.

IMARC: India structured cabling $841.76M in 2025, 8.57% CAGR to 2034, roughly ₹7,500 Cr [40]
The pool is real and CNL's share is under 1%; it is also a copper-priced commodity with 20% gross margin
₹3,000 Cr (May 2026), then ₹2,000 Cr growing 24% a year (Oct 2026) [34][32]

web_blocks.takeaway: Base-year sizes mostly check out, but the growth rates in the deck run at roughly 1.5x to 2x independent estimates; we halve them when sizing runway. [33][40]

web_blocks.text: Market size is not what limits this business; capital and certified supply are. Management says surveillance ‘can easily’ reach ₹2,000 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr in two to three years. [32] The bottom-up facts are much smaller. The two STQC-certified Indian brands CNL distributes, Matrix and Sparsh, turned over roughly ₹250 Cr and ₹400 Cr last year. Infinova India's sales fell from ₹38 Cr to ₹32 Cr, and its first-year target under CNL is ₹75 Cr to ₹80 Cr. The FCI order is ₹35.89 Cr. [35][32][42] Reaching ₹2,000 Cr would need about three times the combined turnover of the two brands it distributes. We therefore give surveillance of at least ₹1,000 Cr by FY29 roughly a one-in-six chance. Most of that probability rests on project work such as BharatNet rather than camera distribution.

Physical capacity is no constraint through ₹6,000 Cr. The standalone company had 202 employees and ₹2,551 Cr of revenue in FY26, about ₹12.6 Cr per head. Employee cost was under 1% of revenue, and the company ran 18+ warehouses and 10,000+ channel partners. [30] What has to scale is the balance sheet and the quality of the people running supplier advances and credit decisions. That is why working capital days, not warehouses, are the capacity KPI.

web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue is the achievable part of the target. The brand mix, which needs 6.3x growth in three years, and the profit margin, which needs to roughly double, are where it stretches. At FY26's 75 days the funding need is about ₹680 Cr. [33][32]

web_blocks.text: Internal accruals can carry a lot of this if working capital behaves. If profit after tax grows 30% a year from ₹70.29 Cr, FY27 to FY29 earnings add up to about ₹365 Cr. That funds the ₹301 Cr to ₹351 Cr extra working capital at 52 to 55 days. It does not fund the ₹679 Cr needed at FY26's 75 days. The CMD said in May 2026 that debt and internal accruals would cover working capital for ‘the next 15 months for sure’. He added that capital would be raised only for an acquisition of at least 30% of the company's size. [34] On 4 November 2026 the board approved the Zicom SaaS purchase at an enterprise value of about ₹50.50 Cr, ₹25 Cr in cash and ₹25.50 Cr in shares. In July it approved a budget of up to $4 million for Infinova. [42] Both sit inside that statement; neither changes the working-capital arithmetic.

web_blocks.caption: Our probability-weighted view of FY29 consolidated revenue (growth rates are three-year CAGRs on FY26 total income of ₹2,717.51 Cr)
rows: Growth fades after H1 FY27's 16.5%; BharatNet slips; market entry grows mid-teens
FY27 about 20%, then 25% to 30% with partial BharatNet billing and WOZOYO at ₹100 Cr to ₹150 Cr
BharatNet on schedule, brand growth near 60%, one acquisition adds revenue
Brand, BharatNet and both acquisitions all land on time
web_blocks.takeaway: Probability-weighted FY29 revenue is about ₹5,280 Cr. The chance of reaching ₹6,000 Cr or more is roughly one in four, and the chance that brands reach 40% of revenue is under one in ten. [33][32]

web_blocks.text: Management itself hedges: the CMD told the October 2026 call that ‘you should not be overconfident’ and that the plan is three initiatives so that at least one works. [32] History says growth of this pace is possible, since revenue compounded at 33% from FY19 to FY26. It also says what that cost: cumulative operating cash flow over those years was −₹328 Cr against ₹241 Cr of profit (Chapter 6). [29] We therefore treat ₹6,000 Cr as a ceiling case for the revenue line and expect a lower number with lower mix and margin. These are business-outcome probabilities, not a view on any security.

web_blocks.takeaway: Four of fifteen commitments were delivered, four partly and seven not. Every delivered item is a 12-month revenue, brand or profit number, and none of the four cash or working-capital promises was met. [38][37][36][35][34]

web_blocks.text: The pattern is consistent and it cuts both ways. Management is good at near-term guidance on things the P&L controls. FY23 revenue beat by 12%. Honeywell hit ₹255 Cr against a ₹230 Cr to ₹250 Cr range and ₹369.61 Cr against ₹360 Cr to ₹370 Cr. FY26 profit of ₹70.29 Cr beat the ₹60 Cr it was pointing to. [36][35][34] It is poor at multi-year structural aspirations and at anything the balance sheet controls. Positive operating cash flow was promised in May 2022 and May 2023, and the first positive year, FY25 at ₹21.86 Cr, was followed by −₹271.88 Cr. [29][30] The PAT margin of 4.5% to 5% has been restated at three calls (August 2023, May 2024, November 2025) with the date pushed out each time. [37][35]

The target itself has also drifted. In May 2023 the plan was ₹500 Cr of licensing by FY26 on ₹2,100 Cr to ₹2,200 Cr of sales. In November 2025 it became ‘50% from our own brand and 50% from market entry’ by 2029. By October 2026 it was ₹6,000 Cr with a 60/40 mix, and the CMD added a 15-month pause on any demerger of the brand business. [38][35][33][34] The CFO's May 2025 working-capital promise and his successor's October 2026 statement that 45 days is not sustainable bracket the problem. Both agree normal is above 50 days, and neither year-end has shown it. [36][32] Our judgement is to take management's 12-month numbers at face value and haircut its three-year aspirations by about half. We would also require a balance-sheet date, not a call, before believing a working-capital claim.

web_blocks.takeaway: The record shows an owner-managed company with stable promoter holding, a clean auditor opinion and small procedural lapses. The open items are a CFO change a month before an adverse cash-flow year, an unreconciled related-party balance and a clarification that arrived late. [30][42]

web_blocks.text: On the FCI letter, precision matters. The original release said CNL had ‘secured’ a ₹35.89 Cr FCI project. The September clarification says FCI is the project authority, the order went to NebulArc, and CNL holds a sub-assigned scope. [42] Nothing in the filings suggests the order does not exist, and its value is 1.3% of FY26 revenue. What it shows is a disclosure habit: headline first, structure later, and a BSE query in between. That habit is a smaller version of the way the ₹3,194.83 Cr BharatNet award was announced. The consortium partner and CNL's share are still undisclosed, and the advance work order is subject to performance security and route-wise work orders. [42]

On management quality overall, our weighting has three parts. There is about a 75% chance that the operators are competent, honest in the numbers they print and good at winning principals and orders. There is about a 60% chance that they under-appreciate how much capital their growth consumes. We put about 70% on disclosure staying one step behind events unless an exchange asks. The auditor opinion, the CRISIL BBB+/Stable reaffirmation in August 2026 and the aged-receivables profile in Chapter 6 support the first judgement. [39][30] The call-by-call record supports the second, and the FCI letter and the CFO change are the evidence for the third. Chapter 6 takes the cash-flow question that this audit leaves open.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a question an old distributor once taught me to ask before I read any income statement: what does this business tell me before it tells me its profit? For Creative Newtech the answer is four things, and you and I are going to follow them through this chapter. Gross margin comes first, because the costs underneath it barely move in a year. Brand share comes second, because it is how the company hopes to escape thin distribution margins. Working capital days come third, because they decide whether a rupee of profit becomes a rupee in the bank. Operating cash flow comes last, because nobody can redefine it. The company's own deck says it plainly: ‘Creative’s business model is primarily of optimizing working capital.’ Keep that sentence in your head, because I am going to hold management to it.

Start with the margin, because the numbers are good. Gross margin was 7.59% in the December 2025 quarter and 12.09% in June 2026, and the market-entry segment, the old low-margin distribution book, doubled its contribution margin from 3.4% to 6.7% in six months. You would normally cheer. I want you to ask what the customer is paying for. The CMD answered on the 15 May 2026 call: ‘While the margin is higher, your expenses are also a bit higher because these are smaller customers, so they can't really have a lot of money for larger orders cash flow.’ Read that slowly. The higher margin is partly a fee for lending money to smaller buyers and suppliers. A margin that arrives together with fatter receivables is not free, and you should never read the one without the other.

Now the brand story, which is the heart of the pitch. Brand revenue was ₹213.39 Cr in the first half of FY27, 17.4% of the total, and 19% in the September quarter. Compare that with about 8% in FY23 and you can see real progress. But walk to the warehouse door and look at the pallets: almost 97% of last year's brand revenue was Honeywell, a licence that, on management's own account, comes up for renewal in March 2027. The CMD has a bar for this business: ‘for us, any brand which is not doing INR1,000 crores is not a brand.’ By that bar the company has one half-brand, one new brand with about ₹20 Cr of sales in its first months, and a newly signed AT&T licence with no revenue. Brand share is, for now, a licence KPI.

Then there is the number I would watch before any other. Net working capital days were 75 at March 2026 and 45 at September 2026. The CFO, Ajit Thakur, was asked on the 29 October 2026 call whether 45 is a steady state, and I want you to notice how plainly he answered: ‘this is not sustainable to come to the level where we have to maintain this kind of level.’ Normal, he said, is 52 to 55 days. So the man who signs the numbers has told you that the best working-capital reading in two years should not be extrapolated. I admire that candour. But it also means you should treat the H1 cash-flow figure as a picture of one afternoon, not a trend, until a later balance sheet repeats it.

Let me take you through a slide, because market-size slides are where optimism hides. The company's deck says India's surveillance market grows 20.6% a year to $12.25B by 2030. Mordor Intelligence puts the 2025 base at $4.40B, close to the deck's $4.80B, but grows it at 9.94%. The deck says India's data-centre capacity was 4.48 thousand MW in 2025; the Council on Energy, Environment and Water says about 1.5 GW. The air-purifier growth claim of 24% sits against IMARC's 13.5%. None of this means the opportunity is small. It means the starting points are honest and the growth rates are about double what outsiders print, so I cut them in half when I think about runway. One more habit to learn: when a number moves inside the same company's own mouth, such as the India air-purifier market going from ₹3,000 Cr in May to ₹2,000 Cr in October, trust the direction of travel less than the existence of a range.

The bottom-up test is more sobering and more useful. The CMD told the October call that surveillance ‘can easily’ do ₹2,000 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr in two or three years. Picture what that takes. The two Indian brands CNL distributes made roughly ₹250 Cr and ₹400 Cr last year between them. Infinova India, the acquisition due to close by mid-November, sold ₹32 Cr last year, and the CMD's own first-year goal is ₹75 Cr to ₹80 Cr. The FCI order is ₹35.89 Cr. You do not get to ₹2,000 Cr by adding up cameras; you get there only if project contracts such as BharatNet are counted as surveillance. So I give surveillance reaching ₹1,000 Cr by FY29 about a one-in-six chance, mostly through projects. That is not an insult to management; it is the difference between a market that is large and a share that is earned one certified product and one reference customer at a time.

Capacity deserves a sentence, because a student of distribution always asks where the bottleneck is. It is not warehouses. In FY26 the standalone company had 202 employees and ₹2,551 Cr of revenue, about ₹12.6 Cr per head, and employee cost was under 1% of revenue. The bottleneck is capital, and then judgement: how much advance to pay a small Indian component maker, how much credit to give a new corporate customer, how many days of stock to hold when memory prices rise 30% to 40%. The CMD described that last choice candidly in May: when material is short, ‘you keep buying whatever material is available.’ Those are decisions that need a seasoned finance function, and the finance function changed hands a month before results. I am not saying the new CFO is the wrong person; he has been candid on his first two calls. I am saying capacity in this business is a people-and-capital question, and you should ask who now owns the credit decisions.

Now the ₹6,000 Cr target, which I want you to treat as arithmetic before you treat it as ambition. From ₹2,700 Cr that is a 30.5% compound rate for three years. If FY27 grows about 20%, as the CMD said on 29 October with the words ‘roughly give and take’, then FY28 and FY29 must each grow 36%. The mix is harsher: brand revenue must go from ₹381 Cr to ₹2,400 Cr, which is 85% a year, while the CMD's own guide is 50% to 60%. The CFO put it simply: ‘So from the INR6,000 crores, 40% is coming INR2,400 crores of revenue.’ At the guided brand growth you land near ₹1,300 Cr to ₹1,560 Cr instead. The funding need, at 52 to 55 days, is another ₹300 Cr to ₹350 Cr, roughly what three years of profit can pay.

So what is my honest probability? I run four scenarios. If growth fades after the first half, FY29 revenue is about ₹4,465 Cr and I give that 35%. A base case of 25% growth gives about ₹5,300 Cr at 40%. Good delivery on BharatNet and brands gives ₹6,100 Cr at 17%, and everything landing together gives nearly ₹7,000 Cr at 8%. The weighted answer is around ₹5,280 Cr, and the chance of ₹6,000 Cr or more is about one in four. The chance that brands reach 40% of sales is under one in ten. The CMD himself warned, ‘you should not be overconfident’. I take him at his word and ask you to do the same.

Now to the part where we put management on trial, and I want you to be fair to them. I read nine earnings calls from May 2022 to October 2026 and listed fifteen specific commitments. Four were delivered, four partly, seven not. Here is the pattern. On 23 May 2022 the CFO said: ‘by September we should be to show a positive cash flow for sure.’ On 29 May 2023 he said again: ‘we will have a positive cash flow this time for sure.’ FY23 operating cash flow was −₹21 Cr and FY24's was −₹28 Cr. On 16 May 2025 the promise was ‘we are going to bring down our working capital from 39 to 35’; the year-end figure was 75. Three promises, one theme, one outcome. That is a pattern, not bad luck.

Now the credit side, because a mentor who only lists failures is not teaching you anything. The same executives said Honeywell would reach ₹230 Cr to ₹250 Cr in FY25, and it printed ₹255 Cr. They said ₹360 Cr to ₹370 Cr for FY26. The CMD recounted the result on 15 May 2026: ‘Our guidance was INR359 crores, INR360 crores. We did INR370 crores.’ In November 2025 he pointed to about ₹60 Cr of profit ‘or slightly better’, and FY26 delivered ₹70.29 Cr. These are one-year numbers where the business controls the outcome, and management has been honest and often conservative on them. So the right reading is that you may trust their 12-month brand and profit guidance and distrust their multi-year margin, mix and cash promises.

Margin promises are where the drift is easiest to see. In August 2023 the plan was a PAT margin of 4.5% to 4.75% by FY25 or FY26. In May 2024 the CFO said ‘within 2 years -3 years the PAT margins will look in the range of 4.5% to 5.56%.’ In November 2025 it was ‘another two, three years’ again. Actual PAT margin was 2.59% in FY26 and 3.20% in the first half of FY27. The target has been about three years away for three years. I do not read bad faith into that; I read an aspiration being repeated as though it were a forecast. The CFO even said in 2024: ‘that's our aspiration, it is not the guidance.’ Investors, not management, are the ones who turned it into an expectation.

Governance is the last piece, and I want to separate what is established from what is merely uncomfortable. Promoters hold 56.62%, steady for two years, and the annual report discloses no pledge. The auditor's opinion is unmodified. The CFO of four years resigned on 14 April 2026 and the new CFO signed the accounts on 14 May. The notes show a related-party balance with Click Retail of ₹47.74 Cr against ₹26.78 Cr of that year's sales, which I cannot reconcile. And the FCI release, headlined as an order from the Food Corporation of India, was clarified on 11 September to say the order came from a systems integrator. None of this is wrongdoing; every item is a question you would ask the audit committee. If you leave this chapter with one habit, let it be this: separate what the record establishes from what it merely leaves unexplained, and write the second list down so that the next quarter's filings can answer it.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When I audit a promoter-run distributor I ask one thing: which of the numbers they promised can they move by themselves? They can move revenue by taking an order, and they did. They cannot move cash by announcing it; that needs a customer to pay and a supplier to wait. The honest scorecard on this call record is a company that is excellent at what it can book and poor at what it must collect, and every chapter that follows rests on that distinction.

book_callouts.title: THE TWO-CLOCK RULE
book_callouts.text: Management runs two clocks. The profit clock runs on orders and margins and ticks to guidance. The balance-sheet clock runs on payment terms and counterparties and ticks to whatever the weakest customer or the strongest supplier will allow. Believe the first clock's 12-month promises. Wait for a balance-sheet date before believing the second clock's.
